## Executive Summary 

###### Chinese acceleration not apparent; major surplus looms 

- As we move into the last two months of 2012, there is no concrete sign that the hoped-for acceleration in Chinese H2 consumption is materialising, and sentiment from market players within the country seems markedly downbeat.  This fact, along with the Eurozone debt crisis continuing to depress the region’s industrial activities and hamper growth elsewhere, has prompted CRU to reduce its estimation of consumption in 2012 by almost 300,000t, and by roughly the same amount in the following years of the forecast period. 

- At the same time, fewer than usual disruptions to supply this year have meant that we have raised our estimate of refined production by 370,000t in 2012.  In particular, we have witnessed significantly lower losses due to labour unrest and ore grade declines over the last nine months. 

- As a result, we now forecast a minor deficit in 2012, after taking into account bonded stock changes this year.  In 2013, we are forecasting that the market will be relatively balanced for the first three quarters before moving into a substantial surplus in Q4, as new production from the 48 mining projects due onstream next year begins to contribute. 

- Due to weaker sentiment, we forecast an average LME cash price of $7,766/t for Q4, which gives an average price of US$7,913/t (US359¢/lb) for 2012.  A balanced market in H1 next yea

r and demand growth in China, Europe and the Americas is expected to drive higher prices, above $8,300/t in the two mid-quarters, before a distinct move into surplus depresses prices in Q4. This leads us to expect a mild increase in the annual average price to just over $8,000/t for the year. - Further out, in 2015, the build-up in new supply from projects is set to push the balance into a heavy surplus of over 500,000t, while prices sink below $7,000/t for the year. With a raw surplus of 700,000t seen for 2016, we believe at this point that prices will fall further, forcing a response from the supply side. We have therefore included a “market-related adjustment” to our supply forecast in 2016 and 2017 to account for expected cutbacks and project delays. |Table I: LME Copp|er price

The 2012 refined copper consumption forecast now stands around 300,000t lower at 19.6Mt, with a similar sized adjustment reducing the 2013 forecast to around 20.4Mt. Further problems in Europe have prompted us to reduce the region’s consumption outlook down by 200,000-250,000t/y, while the Chinese consumption forecast has been revised down by 50,000-70,000t/y. Beyond 2013, the global refined forecast is down by around 320,000t/y. **Supply** : We have increased our expectations for 2012 mined and refined output, as fewer mine disruptions than normal this year mean that we now anticipate refined production growth of 1.8% to 19.8Mt, up from our estimate of 19.5Mt in the July report. In the years 2013-2015, the total changes are minor, amounting to less than 70,000t/y, but in 2016, our production number is now estimated to be lower by almost 500,000t, primarily as a result of lower Chinese production expectations since several smelter/re

finery projects have been cancelled or come under greater scrutiny since our last report. We have also introduced a market-related adjustment in 2016 (and 2017) to take into account likely production cutbacks and project delays due to the growing surplus in the market, and related lower prices. 

**Prices** : Our 2012 annual average price forecast is basically unchanged at just over $7,900/t for LME cash.  Prices for 2013 have been lowered by around $460/t as we are now seeing a greater surplus next year, resulting in higher stock levels.  The 2014 LME cash price has been lowered by $290/t, but the big changes come in the years 2015-2016, as the building surplus drives higher stock:consumption ratios. The forecasts are lower by $770/t and $940/t, respectively, as the 2015 surplus is now expected to be 360,000t higher at 560,000t.  The rollover effect of this surplus will hit 2016’s prices. 

###### LME Week talks bring out China concerns.... 

During our many and varied conversations with industry insiders at 2012’s LME week gettogether in London (15-19 October), the topic of Chinese economic growth was probably the most frequently discussed.  Indicators had become less positive as the year has pressed on, with bodies ranging from the World Bank to the Chinese government downgrading GDP growth expectations for 2012, successive PMI indices showing a rating of below 50, indicating contraction, and numerous stories of rising stocks of cathode, semi-finished products and finished goods. 

Chinese companies themselves added to the gloom, speaking anecdotally of weaker sentiment in the end-use sectors.  Not all the tales matched, however: We were told by some that demand growth for wirerod has declined due to reduced investment in the national power grid, while others maintained that the wirerod and copper tube sectors were not of concern but that flat-rolled copper products demand was suffering.   In any event, despite some discrepancies between viewpoints, the consensus was that the industry in China is experiencing weaker demand growth, and that consumption growth due to private household investments is not as strong as it has been in the past. 

CRU concurs with the broader picture of a slowdown, and having gone into LME week with a consumption growth number of 6.6% for China in 2012 (down from 7.2% in July), we have now

In the short term, we are expecting the completion of the leadership transition in early November to raise domestic confidence, and this should translate into some additional physical demand. CRU agrees with market insiders that the new government will not embark on any new major stimulus packages, being cautious over inflation, but that some smaller measures designed to boost end-use demand will probably be introduced. The effects of some recent subsidy packages (vehicles with engines of 1.3 litres or smaller, etc) are expected to filter through to cathode demand by spring next year, adding to the seasonal increase, and thereby resulting in a boost to consumption and prices throughout the mid-year. ###### ...and most of Europe seen weaker The biggest change to our consumption forecast since July has been the reduction in expectations for Europe in 2012 and 2013 (and beyond in terms of actual tonnages consumed). A study of our European data revealed an overestimation of consumption in 2011 and an overly optimistic forecast of 2012. Following weak apparent consumption data and a host of negative indicators, CRU has amended Europe’s numbers and we now expect a 4.4% y-o-y contraction in refined copper demand in 2012, as Western European consumption declines by 4.1% y-o-y and Eastern and Central European demand falls by 4.9% y-o-y. However, we believe that this region’s contractions are coming to an end, and CRU expects that the refined copper market in Western Europe will reach its bottom before mid-2013 and will start an incomplete rebound to finish the year exhibiting slightly positive annual growth of 0.4% y-o-y.  A recovery in the German manufacturing sector is pivotal in effecting this change as we forecast that German refined copper consumption will be the first major European market to stage a recovery. The economies of Italy, Spain and Greece, having been hit worse by the euro-debt crisis than Germany, are forecast to see copper cathode demand re-emerge more slowly than the latter nation.  In 2012, consumption in Italy, Spain and Greece is predicted to decline by 3.3%, 7.8% and 7.0% y-o-y to represent 30% or 797,000t of Western European refined copper demand.  Following this we expect slower contractions in 2013 of 1.0%, 1.2% and 1.8% as the economies continue to slide downwards in the first half of the year.  West European demand is only expected to rebound properly in 2014, but from this point CRU anticipates 2.5-3.0% growth each year as the economies undergo recovery. 

Some countries in East Europe, such as Poland, are still expected to see growth in 2012, but the E&C Europe regional numbers are affected by lower Russian rod p

roduction this year, as end-use in the West European export markets contracted. Going forward, we see the subregion’s overall demand rebounding, led by Poland and Russia. ###### Price sensitive to macroeconomic developments in 2012 The copper price in 2012 has been primarily propelled by broad macroeconomic sentiments and exchange rate movements. As the chart overleaf indicates, the price has closely tracked the trade-weighted US dollar index in the last year, and this continues, with price falls in the last few days attributed to worries over Europe and China. This tracking behaviour has been largely driven by a relatively balanced market in Q2 and Q3, which saw only slight surpluses, while the supplyside mostly managed to avoid any major outages and few insiders or observers took a strong view either way on the demand outlook, as the market waited for a signal from China’s end-use markets. In September, the announcement of QE3 in the US and a package of stimulus measures unveiled by the outgoing Chinese leadership prompted an investment surge into all markets which buoyed up copper to trade comfortably above $8,000/t from 10th September until 19th October. This was the first time the price had seen an 8 in front of it since May, when a critical mass of investors had decided to short commodities. However, downward movement was triggered on 19th October by copper-specific, or at least commodity-specific, sentiment, as market players and observers gathered in London and broadly agreed that a surplus was on its way and that Chinese demand growth was weaker than had been hoped. The price has traded in the high $7,000s since then, and we are forecasting an average of $7,770/t for the quarter, as the market responds to the downward pressure from the higher surplus expected in Q4 and negative news from China. ###### Incoming supply wave to push 2013 surplus... Alongside our lower expectations of demand in certain key regions, we have also increased our production outlook for 2012 due to unusually fewer incidences of supply outages this year, particularly in the mining sector. We are now forecasting mine production of 16.5Mt of contained copper, up by 2.3% y-o-y and 300,000t higher than in our July report. However, lower disruption in 2012 does not imply that copper mining performance h

as turned a corner and is set to become more reliable, as shown by the early Q3 numbers posted in the last fortnight. While most mines have shown minor deviations from our expectations (both up and down), the world’s third largest copper mine by capacity, Collahuasi, has been experiencing significant difficulties this year, leading CRU to reduce the 2012 estimate to show a 37.5% fall in output, y-o-y. So far, 15 projects have been commissioned in 2012 and a further 19 are due to commence operations in Q4. Most have been small, with just three having output of 100,000t/y or more. Looking ahead, however, 48 copper projects with a total production capacity of 2.5Mt are expected to come onstream in 2013, which will mark the start of the period of rapid expansion in global mine production with annual growth rates in aggregate production in the range of 4- 7% until 2017. In 2013, we project a 6.0% increase in mined copper production, which will drive a 4.1% increase in refined copper production to reach 20.6Mt. With consumption set to grow by 3.7% to 20.4Mt in the same year, we therefore forecast a surplus of over 260,000t. As the chart on the next page indicates, the vast bulk of the surplus is projected to come in at the end of the year, while the first three quarters are expected to see a balanced market. Moving into 2013 and beyond, we indicate the upside and downside risks generated by our price model by showing the price forecasts at the 15th and 85th percentile of iterations. With the exception of 2014, the balance of risk is to the upside, reflecting the persistently erratic mine performance in the copper industry, and periodic unexpected outages in the smelting/refining sector. (Historical disruption figures are among the inputs to our model.) We also note that with the market moving into a situation of high surpluses, we expect to see cutbacks at operations and delays to projects, but our estimates may be too conservative. On the downside, macroeconomic and financial risks and their consequent negative impact on consumption could offset the upside risks of lower copper production and higher investor inflows into copper. ###### **Production risks** Production risks to the price forecast are biased towards the upside. The frequency and variety of outages at mining operations compared to other sectors of the industry are well known, and despite a better year for mine performance in 2012, we have still seen problems with technical failures, labour action and ore grades declining below expectations in certain mines. These risks remain present looking ahead, while incidences of disruption to mines and projects related to “resource nationalism” are on the rise. Alongside the threat from disruption, which we define as an unplanned and unexpected outage, the possibility of cutbacks and project delays due to the economic environment has gained strength lately. Copper miners have enjoyed lengthy periods of the price hovering well above the cost curve in the last decade, and this industry has often been somewhat out of step with the more marginal situation seen by the miners and producers of other metals. However, cost escalation in the last year has been steep, and miners expressed their concerns to us during LME Week. With copper prices around the $8,000/t mark, the vast

majority of miners will remain profitable, but we are aware that certain mines have operating costs above $6,000/t and as the supply surplus begins to bring prices down at the end of the outlook period, we expect some mines to be forced to close and projects to be delayed. We have already built in this projection of cuts into our forecast for Chinese mines specifically, due to their higher average cost profile, and the whole of the supply side with our “market-related adjustment”.  Despite these allowances, it may be that the total cutbacks and delays driven by the market are deeper, and thereby tighten supply to the extent that the price finds support, and potentially moves higher. 

###### **Macroeconomic and financial risks** 

In the last 18 months, the copper price has shown great sensitivity to macroeconomic developments, with most price movements dictated by the release of key indicators, stimulus announcements by governments and institutions, and currency exchange moves.  We therefore see the key risk to the forecast coming from the continued uncertainty over the global economy. Despite better numbers from the US this year, we are not seeing a strong return to growth in China in H2, leaving question marks over the country’s situation, and the Eurozone crisis has continued bubbling.  The safe haven status of the US dollar in a crisis could also see it strengthen faster than we have accounted for in the base case, which would be negative for a dollar denominated price.

###### **Consumption risks** 

###### **Downside** 

Aluminium producers are currently facing challenging conditions, with the industry in a situation of chronic oversupply.  Smelter closures began in the beginning of 2012, with many of the closures directly impacting captive hot metal wirerod plants at aluminium smelters.  So, despite a Cu:Al price ratio of almost 4:1, supply constraints are likely to prevent aluminium from increasing its market share in the rod sector in the short term.  Longer term though, the substitution threat remains significant for copper demand growth in wirerod.  We expect aluminium will make more inroads into the insulated power cable market as a result of an increase in aluminium wirerod capacity available to target this segment by 2015. 

CRU forecasts that the ratio of the copper price to that of aluminium will average close to 4:1, which will weigh on all consumers’ strategic decision-making regarding substituting away from copper. 

###### **Upside** 

The potential shortage of scrap for direct use (due to weaker generation) could lead to additional cathode requirements, especially in China. 

A double-dip recession would only accelerate the emerging markets decoupling their economic growth further from the industrialised countries by favouring copper-intensive domestic demand. 

Some Chinese consumers or the SRB could see copper as a barg

ain for speculative purposes at prices much lower than our base case, thus leading to higher cathode imports.  As a result of RMB appreciation, further support for copper could also emerge from a diversion of surplus cash away from the dollar and directly into commodity investments as a means of diversification. 

If the Chinese government is unsuccessful in curbing the use of copper cathode for financing purposes, then this practice will continue to grow, and bonded warehouse stocks will swell.

###### 3. Regional development 

###### 3.1 Americas 

###### **3.1.1 North America** 

Despite our annual growth estimate for US industrial production this year being revised downwards from 4.4% to 3.4% y-o-y, the refined copper market in the US continues to show good year-on-year growth.  This has been largely due to the ceasing of Russian wirerod imports, but also because of the rapid growth seen in US automotive production.  Mexico, as a major components manufacturing base for the North American automotive industry also benefitted from strong growth in US autos. Combining this with the revival of its copper raw material supply chain has resulted in a fast rise in Mexican refined copper demand as its copper semis industry managed to grow in competitiveness compared with the US industry. 

In the first three quarters of calendar year 2012, apparent consumption of refined copper in the US grew by 1.5% y-o-y.  This breaks down to y-o-y growth of 2.6%, -1.8% and 3.9% for Q1, Q2 and Q3 respectively, with the level amounting to 1.25Mt over the whole period.  The quarterly split of apparent consumption is not an accurate depiction of the real copper cathode consumption that took place in the US market.  The Q1 and Q2 figures have been distorted by physical market manipulation as artificial tightness was introduced through large LME copper cathode stock drawdowns.  This began in Q1, when 103,000t of copper cathode was withdrawn mainly from US metal exchange warehouses.  In Q2 the trend continued as 99,000t of cathode stock was drawn-down, and our Q3 numbers indicate that a further 23,000t of refined copper was released from US exchange warehouses.  This marks a huge change in stocking dynamics from the previous year when destocking/restocking never amounted to more than 13,000t in a single quarter. 

Th

e busier destocking activity this year coincided with higher exports than in 2011 as levels reached 54,000t, 84,000t and 28,000t in Q1, Q2 and Q3, up from 10,000t, 8,000t and 9,000t in the respective quarters in 2011.  In Q1, the 44,000t y-o-y rise in exports accounted for half of the 93,000t growth in destocking, while imports and production only contracted by 34,000t, implying an additional 10,000t of refined copper consumption in the US market. It is our belief that much of this material was in fact stored in offwarrant warehouses.  In Q2, exports made-up a higher proportion of the large stock drawdown, meaning that only 12,000t of the withdrawn copper cathode exchange stocks were available to the US market.  However, production and imports contracted by more than this (19,000t), implying that refined copper consumption fell by 7,000t. ###### 3.2 Europe 

The prospect of seeing the beginnings of a copper demand recovery in Europe this year has quickly faded as apparent consumption data emerged, initially for H1 2012 and then again for Q3 2012.  The data confirmed the grim outlook signalled by leading indicators and market sentiment.  CRU now expects a 4.4% y-o-y contraction in European refined copper demand in 2012, as Western European consumption declines by 4.1% y-o-y and Eastern and Central European demand falls by 4.9% y-o-y.  This leaves the annual European refined copper consumption level resting at 3.7Mt or 18.8% of global demand in 2012, down from 20.2% in 2011. 

###### **3.2.1 Western Europe** 

A study of our European data revealed an overestimation of consumption in 2011 and an overly optimistic forecast of 2012. 

Apparent consumption, as calculated from refined copper production, imports, exports and reported stocking is an essential indicator for monitoring demand.  However, off-warrant stocking, destocking and material-in-transit can skew these figures by a large degree.  Small nations that are often used as trade hubs or for housing stock levels that are high in proportion to their domestic conusmption are more susceptible to distorting trends in apparent consumption away from those of their actual domestic copper cathode consumption.  In Western Europe the **Netherlands** and **Belgium** (amounting to approximately 10% of regional demand) are the two most problematic nations for finding convergence between apparent and reported consumption and as such the demand levels of these countries are analysed in a more rigorous but less regular manner.  CRU will audit these figures in early 2013 in coordination with end-of-year company results. 

Investigating the remaining 90% of Western European demand reveals large y-o-y contractions in consecutive quarters during late 2011 and throughout 2012.  These figures are more pronounced than the decline in actual cathode consumption because a portion of the change in apparent consumption is due to a thinning in offwarrent stocks, including smelter/refinery and semi-fabricator working stocks and non-exchange warehouses.  This behaviour is reflected to some extent in the stock levels of exchange warehouses, which show the copper cathode level as having fallen from 154,000t at the end of Q3 2011 to 117,000t in Q3 2012, a drop of 24% y-o-y.

Our forecast for actual cathode consumption in Germany for full-year 2012 is 1.12Mt, down by 5.0% y-o-y, with the expected 2% greater growth in actual compared to apparant consumption attributed to off-warrant cathode stock drawdowns that were used for consumption. ###### **3.2.2 Eastern and Central Europe**

In 2012, with the decline seen in downstream sectors across Western Europe, the export market for Russian copper products has proven to be much weaker, which has resulted in a large decline in Russian refined copper demand. sion-making until some clarity is apparent from the new government. After a year that has witnessed an unusual level of high-level scandals amongst China’s political elite, we believe that a smooth transition to new leaders in the next CRU International Limited confidential 30 Copper Market Outlook October 2012 Chapter 1 few weeks will lead to an atmosphere of broader assurance and confidence, which should translate into a certain amount of improved physical copper demand. We expect Chinese refined consumption to pick up in H1 next year, as the impact of the recent stimulus measures comes through, as the new leadership inspires confidence, scrap supplies remain constrained by lower availability outside the country, and as the economies of many of China’s more troubled export markets begin to see recovery. However, we see growth decelerating a little further as the market regains strength, and so we forecast a rate of 6.2% next year, down from this year’s figure of 6.4%. In 2014, we expect to see refined consumption growth peak at 7.6%, alongside our IP growth peak, before a long term slow deceleration kicks in, reaching a rate of 5.4% y-o-y in 2017, which equates to consumption of around 11.1Mt. Under our standard probability assumptions and disruption allowance (see appendix D) and before any additional adjustments, mine production would grow at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 5.1% between 2012 and 2017, peaking at 7.1% in 2015, when full capacity production from projects commissioned in 2013 and 2014 percolate into the market. The majority of new production will come from copper concentrates projects, with the result that concentrate output would grow at a CAGR of 6.4% between 2012 and 2017, to reach 17.23Mt in 2017. In contrast, SXEW output is set to experience much slower growth of just 0.5% over the same period, reaching 3.64Mt in 2017. ###### 2.2. Potential disruptions The key development over the last three months has been a marked decline in the incidence of labour unrest so far in 2012 compared to the same period in 2011, with just a handful of shortlived strikes taking place at copper mines. We attribute this decline largely to fewer wage negotiations scheduled for the first three quarters of the year than usual. In addition, mine operators appear to have averted some risks by staging contract negotiations early, although they were also aided by a fall in refined copper prices which helped to reduce tensions with workers. The risk of labour unrest in Q4 has also been averted with the early agreement of new contracts at some major Chilean operations. However, there is the possibility of violent protests spreading from gold and platinum mines in South Africa. With regards to ore grades, our sample of some of the world’s largest copper mines indicates that Q2 2012 marked the continuation of the trend of increasing ore grades that began in Q2 2011, following a glitch in Q1 2012 grades. As miners prepare to reach end-of-year production targets, processing of high grade deposits becomes common practice, which may support grades for the remainder of the year. Ore grades in Australasia remained at the same level as in the previous quarter, although still 3% below the same quarter of 2011, and lower than the long term average. North America exhibited a similar behaviour, with little change q- o-q, while staying at a level below the long term average. South and Central America experienced a significant increase in its average ore grade, of 9% q-o-q and of 18% y-o-y. The increase was influenced by the strong recovery in Escondida’s ore grade, which reached 1.37% in Q2 2012. However, even though ore grades in South and Central America have recovered significantly from the previous year, they are still approximately 25% lower than five years ago. Finally, our sample of European mines not only registered improved ore grades, but reached a level that is higher than five years ago. The increase was 13% q-o-q and 27% y-o-y. Fluctuations in ore grades result from a variety of factors, both planned and unexpected. In recent months, several mines have reported significant changes in ore grades that are the result of processing stockpiled material. This, for example, was the case at Huckleberry, where lower grades were attributed to a significant portion of mill feed coming from low grade stockpiles. In Dikulushi, lower grade stockpiles (accumulated since mid-2010) were processed until February, resulting in higher ore grades afterwards. Other examples include Prominent Hill (the stockpiles will be processed in H2 2012), Batu Hijau, where the effect on production was significant, and Kipoi. Reasons for building and consuming stockpiles are mainly operational, but market prices may also have some bearing on the decision. Faced with declining ore grades, mining companies have also taken investment decisions and made deliberate efforts to fight this trend and counteract its effect on production. A case in point is Escondida, where production recently rose due to the exploitation of a high grade section of the mine, while its Ore Access project, already completed, will provide access to higher ore grades during H2 2012, as well as in the coming years. Escondida’s ore grade in Q2 was 20% above the previous quarter, and 29% above the same quarter of 2011. Escondida expects to increase its production over the next years through a combination of increased throughput and acc

ess to higher ore grades. To achieve this, the company has been developing several projects that required a significant investment. Looking at longer term trends, based on CRU’s annual ore grade data for global committed production, we expect that Africa will continue to register high and increasing ore grades. Perhaps more importantly, after declining at an annual rate of around 6% between 2006 and 2012, South and Central America’s ore grades are stabilizing and are even expected to increase in 2013 by approximately 4% y-o-y in the case of mill operations. However, it is more than likely that new projects coming on stream in the next few years, especially in the more established mining regions, will deflate this average, owing to lower grades prevailing at newer operations due to an ever-increasing deficiency of high grade deposits. Furthermore, the increased economic viability of mining low grade ores due to prevailing high copper prices is set to exert further downward pressure on grades in many regions. However, the threat of strikes in Q4 has receded with the agreement of new labour contracts at Anglo American’s Los Bronces, El Soldado and Chagres operations and Codelco’s Andina. However, there is an increased likelihood of labour unrest at copper mines in South Africa after violent protests broke out in August at platinum and gold mines in the region. ###### **Contract worker strikes** An interesting trend that we have witnessed this year is the increasing incidence of contract worker strikes. Further to contract worker strikes earlier this year at Codelco’s Gaby, Chuquicamata, Andina, Ministro Hales and Radomiro Tomic mines and BHP Billiton’s Escondida mine, we have witnessed a further two contract worker strikes at Codelco’s Andina and Chuquicamata operations, both of which took place in July. Although these contract workers’ strikes did not result in a significant disruption to production, their importance should not be underestimated. Only last year, 10,000 contract workers at Codelco’s El Teniente mine staged a strike spanning almost three weeks, causing production losses of 17,100t of copper. Contract workers are, in general, cheaper and can more flexibly cater for the requirements of a mining operation without increasing the payroll on a permanent basis. As a result, the popularity of hiring contract workers has grown significantly over the last decade. Drawing on the example of Chile, the total number of contract workers at mines has been growing at a proportionately higher rate than that of permanent employees. As a result, the ratio of directly employed staff to contract workers increased from 1:1 in 2001 to 1:2.2 in 2011. However, while contract workers are of great benefit to mining companies, they themselves are denied many of the benefits enjoyed by permanent staff employed by the mining company. In the past few years, we have seen an increasing number of contract workers claiming benefits and being incorporated as members of the permanent staff following campaigns and protests. Some of these changes were even supported by permanent workers. As the ratio of contractors to permanent workers increases, the bargaining power of permanent workers diminishes, as CRU International Limited confidential Copper Market Outlook October 2012 Chapter 2 39 strikes can be undermined using contractors to fill positions. We therefore see a motivation for permanent workers to support contractor strikes and to press for more permanent roles. Thus far, mining companies have been very resistant to addressing the contractors’ concerns, stating

that the matter is an issue between them and their direct employers; however, mounting pressure in light of a tightening labour market and miners’ over-reliability on subcontracted staff presents a climate for change. ###### **Other labour disruptions** In other labour unrest related developments, on 17th July, First Quantum Minerals announced that it had halted production at its Guelb Moghrein copper and gold mine in Mauritania, after mine workers went on strike over pay and violent clashes broke out between the striking workers and police, leaving one worker dead. First Quantum is currently in talks with the unions in a government mediated negotiation process. Although, an agreement has yet to be reached, workers began to return to work on 27th July. First Quantum reported that 12 days of production had been lost as a result of the strike. ###### **Future outlook** The risk of labour unrest in Q4 and the beginning of Q1 2013 has been reduced by the recent agreement of new labour contracts at Anglo American’s Los Bronces and El Soldado mines and Chagres smelter, and at Codelco’s Andina mine ahead of the November 30th and December 1st deadlines. These may set a precedent for the negotiations at Codelco’s Chuquicamata operations where the contracts expire in February 2013. We are aware of several negotiations still taking place, however. Talks are underway at the Antamina mine, where labour contracts expired in July, as well as at Southern Copper’s operations in Peru (Cuajone, Toquepala and Ilo) where labour agreements ended in late August. Although negotiations at all of these operations appear to have been prolonged, to date, we have not heard of any strike threats. We believe that the outcome of these may set a precedent for negotiations at other mines in the region. CRU International Limited confidential 42 Copper Market Outlook October 2012 Chapter 2 ###### **2.2.3. Government issues** Over the past year, copper mining companies have encountered increasing c

hallenges from ‘resource nationalism’ around the world.  The last three months have been no exception, with the announcement of a number of government initiatives aimed at boosting state revenue from copper mining.  These included continuing reforms of the Indonesian mining policy, the intention of the Zambian government to increase its stake in copper mining companies, the proposal of the Philippine government to increase royalty charges, and the DR Congo’s review of the mining tax system.  Moreover, many governments have also taken a tougher stance against the mining industry in protecting the environment and indigenous populations.  We have seen instances of such policies in Chile and Peru over the last quarter.  Please note that we discuss government policies specifically affecting copper mine projects in the _Mine projects – recent developments_ section of this report. 

###### **Resource nationalism** 

Further to the Indonesian government’s introduction of a 20% tax on exports of ore that came into effect at the end of Q2 2012, the government has been actively seeking to reap further gains from the copper mining industry.  On 20<sup>th</sup> September, it asked Freeport McMoRan, the owner of the Grasberg mine, to increase its export royalty payments to 10%.  The move comes as part of a review by a governmental commission assembled in January 2012 which has until December 2013 to re-evaluate the nation’s mining policies. Earlier in the quarter, Freeport McMoRan was asked by the government to divest a 51% stake in the Grasberg mine to state.  The company responded by agreeing to divest 9.36% of the mine’s ownership.  The mining sector currently contributes approximately 12% to the nation’s annual economic output.  We perceive the government’s initiatives to increase revenue from the mining sector as highly risky, with the short term benefits of increased state income being potentially outweighed in the long term by investors’ reluctance to enter into a highly uncertain business environment. 

In Zambia, on 25<sup>th</sup> July, the government announced that it plans to increase its ownership stake in mining operations in the country to as much as 25%.  However, it is unclear whether this will apply to all mining operations.  Mines Minister Christopher Yaluma said: “We don’t have any intentions to raise our ownership in most of the mining houses.” Earlier announcements by the Ministry of Mines suggested that the government was seeking to gain 35% ownership of mining operations, but this plan was abandoned.  The Zambian government currently holds a 10-20% stake in most mining operations in the country through ZCCM Investment Holdings Plc.  Two weeks later, on 8<sup>th</sup> August, the Zambian Mines Minister purportedly announced that the government will repeal the mining licences of companies which have failed to create employment.  Zambia National Broadcasting Corp. reported that notices had already been issued. 

Meanwhile, in the Philippin

es, the government completed its review of the mining law in June, but a new mining tax has yet to be passed by Congress.  Currently a 2% excise duty is paid on net profits, but it is proposed to introduce a royalty of between 5 and 7%.  A proposal for a 7% single levy for all mining operations is under consideration by the department of finance.  There are currently five copper concentrate producing mines in the Philippines and they are expected to produce 65,000t of copper-in-concentrate in total in 2012.

###### **<mark>Policies concerning the environment and indigenous populations</mark>** 

In Chile, authorities recently drafted a legal framework around the ILO-convention 169, which gives certain rights to indigenous populations regarding the use of their land.  The new law proposes that indigenous populations will participate throughout the entire project evaluation process.  Although their opinions on the project will not be legally binding they will feed into the SEA’s assessment and will influence its outcome.  The proposed framework bears some similarities to that already in place in Peru. 

Meanwhile, the Peruvian government has indicated that it is taking a tougher stance on environmental issues following a pipeline rupture at the Antamina copper mine in June and a spill of mining waste at the Atacocha zinc mine in late August.  On 4<sup>th</sup> September, the Peruvian Environment Minister Manuel-Pulgar Vidal announced that the government is working to double the maximum possible penalty that can be levied on polluting companies.  Under current legislation, fines run from 2-30M soles (US$0.77-1.15M).  Previously, on 30<sup>th</sup> August, it was announced that the president had sent a bill to Congress that would put the Ministry of Environment in charge of a new committee that would be charged with approving the mitigation plans for new projects and this power is to be taken from the Ministry for Mines.  Both of these initiatives are likely to highlight the importance of environmental issues in mining. 

###### **2.2.4. Infrastructure** 

There were no significant disruptions to actual output related to infrastructure during Q3 2012. However there was a strike by dockworkers at the Port of Antofagasta.  The workers went on strike on 30<sup>th</sup> August in a dispute over wages.  A significant part of Chile’s copper exports pass through the port and the

work stoppage likely affected copper shipments.  The strike lasted 23 days until 25<sup>th</sup> September. 

Power supply continues to be one of the key challenges to future copper production, particularly in Chile.  Low ore grades, water scarcity, and deep deposits are reasons commonly cited as causing energy requirements to increase, both for existing and new mining operations. Although no disruptions were reported during Q3 2012 related to power cuts, mining executives have warned about possible project delays caused by unavailability of power supply. 

Reports emerged in September that PanAust and Codelco had postponed their Inca de Oro copper and gold project due to higher energy costs.  Construction at the $600 million Inca de Oro project was scheduled to begin in 2013 and would have produced 40,000 ounces of gold and 50,000 metric tons of copper a year at full capacity.  Codelco also announced that it has put a decision on expansion plans for its Salvador division on hold until it can secure access to competitive power.

Energy projects are facing strong opposition in Chile, both from the population and from environmental NGO’s.  In August, one of the most significant power generation projects, the $5.3B Castilla coal-fired power plant (and associated port), was suspended by a ruling of Chile’s Supreme Court. As a result, mining companies are likely to become increasingly involved in the energy sector in Chile. 

Opposition to coal and hydro based power plants is having another side effect, making investment in gas-fired plants more attractive.  The availability of cheap shale gas from the United States is also helping their case in Chile.  GasAtacama recently announced that it will invest US$350M in a Floating Storage Regasification Unit (FSRU) seaport in northern Chile, of at least 500MW. 

In Asia, Rio Tinto is in negotiations with a Chinese state-owned utility to secure electricity to start production at Oyu Tolgoi.  The power transmission infrastructure needed to carry electricity across the border from China to the Oyu Tolgoi project has already been built.  The company is optimistic of reaching a satisfactory conclusion to the negotiations, considering that its customers will predominantly be Chinese smelters.  However, a deal has yet to be signed, prompting us to move the project’s starting date back in our forecast from Q1 to Q2 next year. 

In Africa, Zambia will invest US$120M to repair a railway line linking it with South Africa. Zambia exports its copper mainly through the port of Durban in South Africa.

###### **2.2.6. Natural Hazards** 

There have been few significant disruptions to copper mine production during Q3 2012 due to natural hazards.  In Q3 2012 mining operations generally avoided weather-related disruptions, which were significantly more severe during the same period last year. 

One exception occurred in the Philippines, where operations at Philex Mining’s Padcal Mine were halted on 1<sup>st</sup> August after heavy rains caused the mine’s tailing pond to overflow, threatening to contaminate one of the country’s largest rivers.  The spill was contained, but operations at the mine remain suspended.  Philex Mining announced it will build new tailings ponds, but didn’t specify when production would resume.  The Padcal mine was expected to produce 17,000t of copper-in-concentrate in 2012.

###### **2.2.7. Technical failures** 

There have been few reports of major technical disruptions to mine production in the last quarter.  The main developments are summarised below. 

In late July, a pipeline transporting concentrat

e from Antamina’s mine site in the Peruvian Andes to the filtration and port facilities on the coast sprung a leak, causing 3t of material to escape into the surrounding area.  According to reports, local villagers volunteered to clean up to prevent the spillage reaching an important local water source, but over 100 people later began to suffer from a range of ailments including vomiting, headaches and nausea.  A government investigation into the incident is now under way and the operator Minera Antamina is facing a fine of at least 2M soles (~US$769,000) from the regional government of Ancash.  The company has said that it is talking to local leaders to try to resolve the issues that have arisen from the leak.  It is uncertain whether the leak has had an impact on production. 

Another pipeline failure occurred at the Ok Tedi mine in Papua New Guinea in September.  We have heard reports that the operation experienced a blockage of the concentrate pipeline, which took approximately seven days to clear.  The technical failure is said to have resulted in a ten day delay in concentrate shipments from the mine.  Furthermore, the in-pit crusher at the mine also experienced a technical failure around the same time, and will be down for at least two weeks.  Ore stockpiles at the operations are insufficient to keep the mill running for longer than 2-3 days in the absence of a crusher, posing the threat of further production delays. 

Lastly, Newcrest Mining announced in mid-September that it had incurred a temporary disruption at Ridgeway, part of Cadia Valley, following a conveying system failure.  The incident, which took place on 11<sup>th</sup> September, was expected to take 15 days to repair.  During this time, the ore processing plant will be fed with low grade stockpiled ore.  The mine operator expects a production loss of 100-200t of copper-in-concentrate.

Peru has the potential to move into the No. 2 position, boasting many of the largest copper projects in the world that are due to come on stream within the next five years, cumulatively adding 1.1Mt of contained copper capacity by 2017, after all adjustments. Eight of these projects will exceed 100,000t/y contained copper production, with four expected to produce in excess of 200,000t/y. They include Xstrata’s 400,000t/y Las Bambas project, the 270,000t/y expansion of Freeport McMoRan’s Cerro Verde mine, Chinalco’s 250,000t/y Toromocho project, and finally, Anglo American’s 225,000t/y Quellaveco project. Two African nations, Zambia and the DRC, could also potentially move up in the league table. Projects in both countries are expected to add over 0.6Mt/y of contained copper capacity by 2017, after all adjustments. However, it must be noted that greater uncertainties surround projects in Africa compared to more developed regions, posing a greater threat of delays or cancellations. Meanwhile, China is set to be demoted by one position, with Russia, Australia and Canada dropping by two positions each. ###### **Disruptions to project developments** Mine projects have continued to suffer from delays and obstacles to development over the last three months, with increased reso

urce nationalism and concerns over environmental issues and local opposition becoming major impediments, in addition to rising capital costs, a shortage of skilled workers and equipment and technical challenges.  The main developments are summarised below. 

###### **Social and environmental issues** 

A number of major projects have encountered severe setbacks over the last six months as a result of intensifying social and environmental protection restrictions imposed by local and central governing bodies, particularly in South America.  Early May saw the first instance in recent history where a local community has halted the development of a major mining project. The environmental permit for Xstrata’s 130,000t/y copper-in-concentrate El Morro copper-gold project in Chile was suspended following a filing by the Comunidad Agricola Los Huasco Altinos (CAHA) which stated that the community had not been sufficiently consulted over the effects of the project as stated by the International Labour Organisation (ILO) 169 Convention on Indigenous and Tribal Peoples (enacted in 1989). 

Since the ruling, construction activities have ceased at the project site, and the project’s owners are currently working closely with the SEA to comply with the requirements of the ILO 169 Convention.  It could take about 18 months to resume development work, according to local press reports.  Following the suspension of the project, the head of CAHA announced that the group will demand consultation for other projects, including the Relincho (Teck), Pachuy (Barrick Gold) and Paso de la Flecha projects.  Other copper mine projects in the region are Pascua Lama (Barrick Gold), Caserones (Lumina Copper) and Cerro Casale (Barrick Gold, Kinross Gold) which could also be exposed to a similar impediments. 

More recently, in August, under similar circumstances, the Peruvian government announced that it had suspended Newmont Mining’s 90,000t/y copper-in-concentrate Minas Conga project

The government added that Newmont now has two years to conceive of a way to guarantee the supply of water to local residents.  Newmont has stated that in the meantime it will continue with construction of water reservoirs to serve the local communities.  The miner had previously hoped to begin production at the mine by early 2015. 

These developments mark a significant setback to project developers in Peru. In particular, it demonstrates the present government’s sympathy towards local communities and also represents a change of heart on the part of the leftist President Ollanta Humala, who had previously been more supportive of copper mining project.  Further to this development, on 30<sup>th</sup> August it was announced tha

t the president had sent a bill to Congress that would put the Ministry of Environment in charge of a new committee that would be charged with approving the mitigation plans for new projects.  This would give the Ministry of Environment more power to affect the decisions on approvals of new project, which is likely to highlight the importance of environmental issues in the process of obtaining mining permits. 

Another setback on environmental grounds in South America, occurred at Barrick Gold’s binational 5,000t/y copper-in-concentrate Pascua Lama gold, silver and copper project located on the Chile-Argentine border which has been impeded after the Argentine National Supreme Court overturned a preliminary injunction issued by a local government which permitted the project to go ahead despite not conforming to all terms of the 2010 National Glacier Protection Act.  The National Glacier Act prohibits any mining activities taking place in close proximity to glacial and periglacial areas.  Barrick Gold maintains that the permit it received from the San Juan local government is legally binding and that it intends to continue construction work in spite of the Supreme Court’s ruling.  Although the Pascua Lama project has a relatively small copper production capacity, the decision of the Argentine National Supreme Court may set a precedent for more significant copper developments in the region, in particular Xstrata’s 280,000t/y contained copper El Pachon project and McEwen Mining’s 160,000t/y Los Azules copper project in San Juan.  Similarly to Pascua Lama, El Pachon is also located on the ChileArgentine border, and is based in an area susceptible to glaciation.  Projects in this region are likely to be facing delays and capital increases due to the unclear legislation. 

Another interesting development has been that Teck Resources has temporarily withdrawn its SEIA (Social and Environmental Impact Assessment) application for its US$5.6B Quebrada Blanca Phase 2 project in Chile.  The development, which was expected to be commissioned in 2016 prior to the announcement, will eventually replace the current SXEW operation.  The reason for the withdrawal of the SEIA application, however, remains unclear. 

Outside South America, Sagittarius Mines, a subsidiary of Xstrata, warned in August that the start-up of the Tampakan project in the Philippines may be delayed due to regulatory and security concerns.  The government refused to grant environmental clearance to the company, which is likely to result in a delay to the scheduled construction start date in 2013.  The coppergold ore body is situated in a province that has been protected by a mining ban since 2010 which can only be lifted by a court order.  In addition, security concerns have slowed Sagittarius’ field activities following the death of a security guard after a shooting at the site in June, which came only one month after a similar incident resulting in injuries to a guard. ###### **Economic setbacks** 

Further to environmental and social impediments to project developments, uncertainties in the global economic outlook and concerns over rising production costs have also set back a number of copper projects.  BHP Billiton’s announcement that it does not plan to approve any spending on major projects this fiscal year has been the most significant instance of this mounting obstacle.  The company’s decision means that a total of US$68B of planned project expenditure will be put on hold, including the 5-stage expansion of the Olympic Dam mine, which was due to add approximately 575,000t/y of copper-in-concentrate capacity upon completion.  The project’s suspension will have significant implications on future concentrate output from Australasia, with no other project in the region matching the combined output expansion plans of the mine. 

A further example of cost inflation in mining investment was Codelco’s announcement in October that the total estimated investment required for its Ministro Hales mine has increased to US$3.5B from an earlier estimate of US$2.3B. MMH is an important addition to Codelco’s operations, as it will allow the company to retain its leadership in production while output is declining at its existing operations. Production was scheduled to start up in Q4 2013, but local news sources suggest that production could begin earlier. As a result of the discovery of additional oxide reserves during pre-stripping, total expected production could reach 200,000t/y of contained copper until 2015, surpassing the initial forecast of 170,000t/y 

There have also been some project ownership changes.  Lumina Copper has announced the possible sale of its Taca Taca project in Argentina.  This follows a drop in the company’s share price following the Argentine government’s seizure of the YPF SA oil company and concern over the security of investme

nts within the country’s natural resource sector. 

###### **Resource nationalism** 

Further to targeting existing operations as sources of revenue, as the wave of copper mining projects due for commissioning approaches, many governments are increasingly seeking to maximise their interest in these projects in order to secure future sources of revenue.  This year, we have seen this approach adopted by governments in many parts of the world, most notably, Indonesia, Zambia, the DR Congo and the Philippines. 

Most recently, in mid-October, Turquoise Hill Resources, together with Rio Tinto Group and

Turquoise Hill (Rio Tinto 51%) owns 66% of Oyu Tolgoi, while the Mongolian government owns the remaining 34%. This is the second attempt by the Mongolian government to renegotiate the mining agreement.  Last year’s attempt focused on increasing the government stake in the project closer to 50%, but was repealed by both companies. Given last year’s experience, the Mongolian government doesn’t appear to have much leverage in enforcing changes to the original investment agreement.  However, presidential elections are due in seven months’ time and the project may be put in the spotlight once again, especially considering its political and economic significance for the nation. 

###### **Other disruptions** 

Problems in securing power supply have emerged as a major constraint to copper mining projects in many parts of the world.  In recent months, two copper projects have been affected by this obstacle: Oyu Tolgoi and the Salvador expansion. 

Although Turquoise Hill Resources announced in early October that the construction of its Oyu Tolgoi project in Mongolia is “essentially complete,” a key element of the project, the power purchase agreement (PPA) has not yet been agreed.  The company is currently continuing negotiations over the PPA with the Chinese authorities; however, it remains unclear when a settlement may be reached. Oyu Tolgoi is the largest copper mining project anticipated for commissioning next year, and further delays would have a significant impact on the concentrates balance and the availability of concentrates for Chinese smelters. 

Meanwhile, Codelco announced in the same month that it has taken the decision to put the expansion plans for its Salvador division on hold.  The decision comes as a result of the company’s failure to negotiate a “competitive” power agreement.  The company blames Chile’s Supreme Court’s decision to suspend the US$5.0B thermoelectric Central Castilla power project in the Atacama region for contributing to the undersupply of energy. 

Although the additional production from the Salvador expansion is fairly insubstantial, considerin

g the size of Codelco’s other copper projects, the development underlines the risk to mining projects from Chile’s inadequate power supply infrastructure. It remains uncertain how the nation will deal with the wave of mining projects due to come on stream over the next few years, in light of setbacks to a number of power projects, most notably the 2,750MW HidroAysen hydroelectric plant, which is facing fierce environmental opposition. We expect to see delays to projects throughout the production chain, so while we are anticipating delays to mine projects, we expect that this will be matched by delays to smelter and refinery projects and the closure of inefficient and uncompetitive smelting capacity.  Thus while mine project delays will put pressure on concentrate availability, concentrate requirements will also be reduced. 

With regards to production from scrap, the global scrap market remained very quiet in July and August 2012.  From the demand side, an uncertain global economic outlook in conjunction with the holiday period in Europe and the Americas constrained consumption, whereas on the supply side, copper scrap merchants were reluctant to release material into the market due to low refined copper prices.  Generation was also constrained by the global economic recession. These conditions maintained the market in balance, keeping discounts flat.  This situation took a turn in early September, when the substantial increase in refined copper prices on positive economic news in the US and China had a profound impact on the global copper scrap market. Merchants began to free material onto the market, but, we believe that their willingness to sell at higher prices was not mirrored by a similar level of increase in demand, causing scrap discounts to widen in all regions.  Although scrap demand improved from levels observed in July and August, it remains suppressed by high stocks of finished goods in China and continuing economic uncertainties worldwide.  Overall, we expect total production from scrap at smelters and refineries to grow by 3.7% y-o-y to 3.6Mt in 2012.

From a regional perspective, at 75.9%, Asian smelters excluding China are expected to see the highest utilisation rates this year, with Japanese smelters at the forefront, recording rates exceeding 86%. However, when Chinese smelters are factored into the equation, the overall Asian smelting utilisation rate falls to just 69.6%. Chinese smelters are faced with significant difficulties in obtaining raw materials as a result of having to operate in a fiercely competitive market and through lacking established channels with suppliers of raw materials as well as poorer access to credit needed to secure this material. In addition, weak refined copper demand together with the unfavourable SHFE/LME arbitrage has resulted in some Chinese smelters choosing to reduce output rather than compete for concentrates. Furthermore, Chinese producers in recent years appear to have been over-zealous in their ramp-up estimates, which have further contributed to the deterioration in utilisation rates in the region. nd North America are expected to perform well this year, reaching, 72.3% and 71.7%, respectively.  Like the Japanese, smelters in these regions benefit from well established concentrate supply chains from the world’s largest miners. 

At the other end of the scale stand African and South and Central American smelters.  We expect smelting utilisation rates to reach just 61.5% in Africa this year, while we forecast South and Central American smelters to narrowly outperform these, operating at 63.8% of capacity. Chile, the leading South American blister producer, has been performing particularly poorly this year, due to problems at some Codelco operations, most notably the Chuquicamata smelter. Nevertheless, we expect that utilisation rates in the nation will rebound to almost 70% by next year, which should lift up the regional average.

###### **3.2.2 Raw material availability** 

###### **Concentrates** 

We believe that the concentrate market in Q3 has been well balanced, following a slight surplus in Q2. We currently expect that the shortfall in copper-in-concentrate availability in 2012 will amount to approximately 113,000t.  Much of this has already happened; Q1 saw a deficit of 139,000t when mine supply was still struggling to meet commitments.  Since then, the market has eased, due to improvements in mine supply combined with a fall in smelter requirements. Concentrate production this year is expected to be over 200,000t higher than anticipated in July, owing to fewer than expected mine disruptions, predominantly from labour unrest and ore grade declines.  We have reduced our mine disruption allowance to 5% for the remainder of the year. 

With respect to changes in concentrate demand, we anticipate that smelters will require 12.88Mt of copper-in-concentrate this year, up by 233,000t from our July report. We attribute this change to smelters increasing utilisation rates due to better than expected availability of raw materials. 

Looking ahead, we maintain our view that the fundamental imbalance in the market will persist over the next four years, with mined concentrate production continuing to fall short of smelter requirements, and planned smelter output will need to be adjusted downwards.  However, we anticipate that the concentrates market will move into a small surplus by 2017, with production from a wave of mining projects finally catching up with smelter demand.  Additionally, we have reduced the annual deficits forecast up until 2016 due to slower predicted Chinese smelter capacity growth and the cancellation of some major smelting projects. 

It is also worth noting that declining concentrate grades have become a key concern for smelters in recent years.  The average copper grade was not so long ago considered to be around 30%, but as grades have been in retreat for several years this is becoming the exception rather than the rule.  The f

alling grades have been particularly noticeable amongst the Chilean mines. Even well known high-grade operations such as Los Pelambres have lost form and are unlikely to regain it. On a long term basis, average copper content of exported Chilean material has been falling annually (please see chart below), and it appears that 2012 will be no exception. In the first eight months of 2012, grades of concentrate shipped from Chile averaged 29.1%, against a 2011 average of 29.8%. More recently, the latest data indicates average concentrate grades of 27.6% in August for material shipped from Chile, marking a substantial deviation from the year-to-date average of 29.1%. The greatest fall was witnessed in material shipped from Anglo American Sur’s operations, where July grades declined by 5.1pp from the 2011 average to just 22.9% copper content. Meanwhile, grades of concentrate exported from Los Pelambres, Candelaria and Anglo American Norte’s operations all declined by between 2.2pp and 3.5pp from their 2011 average. Additionally, new mines entering the market tend to have percentage concentrate grades in the mid-20s, while several of the largest and most important custom mines are believed to be suffering from grade declines. Lower copper content is not the only problem either - the proportion of impurities is also on the rise. The spot concentrates market in Q3 experienced a surfeit of complex concentrates which require blending before they can be processed. The effect on smelters is that their metal production capacity is being reduced along with average concentrate grades since they have a finite raw material intake capacity. According to market insiders, Chinese scrap merchants have accumulated vast stocks of copper scrap during the first two months of Q3, in spite of struggling domestic demand for the material. Imports of copper scrap into China reached 428,777t in July and 438,146t in August – some of the highest levels in recent years.  This stockpiling of material was primarily driven by an optimistic price outlook for Q4 2012 and beyond, with the anticipation of a seasonally strong Q4, and a widespread expectation of imminent announcements of new economic stimulus packages by the Chinese government in light of numerous indications of slowing economic growth. 

These expectations were realised in early September, when prices increased on positive economic news in China and the US, resulting in large quantities of scrap being released onto the market by merchants.  However, we believe that the suppliers’ heightened willingness to sell was not matched by a similar increase in demand, resulting in a substantial easing of the market

idened substantially as merchants released more material onto the market on higher refined copper prices. ###### **Technical issues** 

In July, Codelco’s Chuquicamata smelter underwent 53 days of maintenance.  We have heard from market insiders that the maintenance was brought forward as a result of problems with the lining of the flash smelter akin to clots in an artery that slowed down the working of the furnace. 

###### **Environmental/Government issues** 

In July, Codelco announced that it plans to invest US$300M to improve sulphur capture at its El Teniente smelter in order to conform to the industry’s environmental standards.  Chilean law stipulates that smelters are required to capture 95% of sulphur emissions, but the El Teniente smelter currently captures only around 93%.  This step is part of a more general US$1B investment project by Codelco to improve the environmental standards at all its operations. 

###### **3.2.4 The sulphuric acid market** 

Activity in the sulphuric acid market was slow in Q3 2012, and particularly in September, as players across Europe, Asia and the Americas were involved with the Q4 and 2013 negotiations. There were signs of demand weakness in several regions, and particularly in China, as well as concerns over the economic situation in Europe. 

In Europe, the majority of contracts for Q3 and H2 were concluded in the €70-80/t range, a rollover from H1.  August saw little extra activity, while during September contract negotiations

The market in the Americas softened during Q3 2012 and, as in Europe, there was little activity, especially as the negotiations for the 2013 contracts started in September.  Demand from Brazil slowed, but spot activity is expected to increase in the coming months with the beginning of the fertilizer season.  Prices in Brazil have moved from around US$90/t cfr at the beginning of the quarter, to around US$100/t cfr for the latest round of business. Despite lengthy talks at the last TFI conference, held between 9th and 12th September in Boston, MA, there was little tangible progress for Chile's 2013 sulphuric acid contracts. US buyers continue to receive offers for November tonnage in the mid-US$90s/t cfr, while some October tonnage was secured at US$95/t cfr US Gulf. 

In Asia, demand in China is weak, but supply has been also constrained with key suppliers in Korea and Japan claiming low production due to turnarounds keeping spot business at a minimum.  In Korea's case, low stock levels are adding to the lack of spot availability, despite interest from several South East Asian buyers.  In Japan, the Tamano smelter is now expected to shut for maintenance from 1st November to 14th December. 

Due to lack of demand in China, suppliers such as Two Lions turned to the international spot market to fix business, with the sulphur-burnt acid producer concluding business recently with Australia at around US$60/t fob. Quotations for acid in Eastern China were in the range of RMB250-500/t cfr at the end of September. 

Contractual talks over Q4 volumes between Japan/South Korea and China were ongoing during September, but stalled over a wide disparity in price ideas, with suppliers holding out for low to mid US$60s/t cfr and buyers aiming for mid to high US$40s/t cfr. The concentrates balance After showing a deficit in the first few months of the year, concentrate supply and demand has been more evenly matched in recent months and the market has moved into balance. This has come about through the combination of improved mine performance with few disruptions but disruptions to smelter output which have resulted in additional concentrates becoming available on the spot market. The key ones of note are the 6-month closure of the Leyte smelter, technical problems at Chuquicamata in Chile, followed by a 53-day maintenance closure, a one-month maintenance closure at Ilo as well as some maintenance closures in China. In addition, Yunnan Tin’s new greenfield smelter suffered from technical problems on start up and is slowly building up to capacity. Looking ahead, we maintain our assumption of a fundamental shortfall in concentrate availability over the next four years, but we see the market flipping into surplus in 2017 as new mine supply finally catches up with smelter requirements. However, once again our near term deficit has been revised downwards. For 2013, this is the result of downward revisions to forecast smelter output, largely in China, as a consequence of slower growth in cathode demand which we believe will impact on smelter output and concentrate requirements. Our forecasts of mine output have been increased in 2014 and 2015, but for 2016 a combination of lower mine output and higher smelter demand means that the concentrate deficit has opened up again compared to our previous forecast. ###### Deficit to persist until market swings into surplus in 2017 Mine concentrate prod

Throughout the year there has been a wide discrepancy between terms for clean and terms for complex material, with the latter being placed at terms upwards of $100/10¢. The market remains long in complex concentrates, which is putting increased pressure on clean material required for blending. More than one trader in today’s market is apparently oversupplied in material that requires blending before a smel

ter can accept it, leading to more aggressive bidding when clean material has been tendered. Even though the market is apparently in agreement that mine/trader terms are now in the $60/6¢s for good quality material, mines with high grade concentrates have been recently insisting that they can secure terms of sub$50/5¢. With average copper grades declining at some key custom suppliers, the quality issue is not just a matter of complex versus clean; the copper grade is also important. We expect that this will feature in the frame contract negotiations and miners with high grade concentrates will be looking to secure lower terms. Trader/smelter terms have also risen over the period, although the gap between miner/trader and trader/smelter terms has narrowed. Demand in China has remained lacklustre due to slow cathode demand and the unfavourable arbitrage. Imports have risen year-on-year, however, and were at a record level in August, partly reflecting the high volume of mine tenders during Q2 but also the increased level of business done on a long term or annual rather than spot basis. Trader/smelter terms in China in late October were reported to be in the $60/6¢s. ###### **Contract Terms** Opening discussions have taken place in the negotiations over frame contract TC/RCs; market views have been exchanged but at the time of writing no numbers have yet been put on the table. BHP Billiton is again pressing for six monthly or even quarterly setting of terms, but the Japanese smelters are believed to be strongly resisting such a move and would apparently require a significant increase in terms to persuade them to make such a move. Due to the different game being played by BHPB, other market players are disregarding their moves and focussing on Freeport and the major Chilean miners. Market insiders speculate that the miners will be starting at roll-over or just below while the smelters will be putting numbers upwards of $75/7.5¢ on the table. The smelters argument for higher TC/RCs is fourfold, citing: the recent easing of the spot market with good concentrate availability and rising TC/RCs; expectations of new mine supply coming on stream in 2013; slowing demand for refined copper in China that will discourage smelters from bringing on new capacity; and the strengthening of the Yen and RMB which is raising smelters’ costs in US$ terms. Miners, on the other hand, argue that the market is still fundamentally short of concentrates, particularly clean, high grade qualities and a recovery in smelter output in Japan, the Philippines and Chile is expected, as well as new capacity start-ups in China. As indicated above, quality will be an issue, and we expect to see a range of terms negotiated for different qualities. As August drew to a close, the markets began to hope that the annual meeting of central bankers held in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, which has long been a forum for the launching of new Fed initiatives, might result in QE3. Although the speech by Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke on 31st August clearly indicated that the Fed was willing to look at a variety of measures to boost market confidence and support economic growth, the markets were disappointed that QE3 was not yet on the table. The tide turned on 7th September, when European Central Bank President Mario Draghi announced that the ECB stood ready to buy bonds from Eurozone member countries, effectively creating a sovereign debt bailout fund to function alongside the existing instruments for helping the region’s banks to regain their footing. (Note that Draghi had skipped Jackson Hole to prepare for the ECB regular meeting). On the same day,

China’s central government announced that it would commit $157B to launching 60 planned infrastructure projects that were stalled due to a lack of regional government funds. CRU International Limited confidential Copper Market Outlook October 2012 Chapter 3 81 These two announcements together changed the tide of market sentiment. Copper prices began to rise as investors perceived that the Chinese and European economies would soon stabilise, and would only improve in the future. The Fed’s announcement of QE3 on 13th September solidified the shift in market sentiment, and sent the euro to $1.312/€ (€0.762/$) on 14th September, its highest level since 4th May. The LME 3-month copper price broke out of its trading range after the ECB announcement on 7th September. It climbed to an intraday high of $8,422/t on 19th September and did not close below $8,000/t until 22nd October when renewed concerns over Spain’s debt crisis began to weigh on the euro once again. ###### Lacklustre demand, higher mine output create oversupply Copper market participants had a variety of reasons to be less than enthusiastic about market conditions. The ongoing uncertainty surrounding the Eurozone’s debt and banking crises along with the lack of momentum in China’s economy reduced economic activity in the rest of the world because companies did not want to risk taking new hiring decisions or implementing capital spending plans in an environment of such high uncertainty. Spot market demand for copper was, therefore, listless during the summer, and lower spot premiums reflected that contract volumes were adequate to meet demand. Mine production continued to surprise to the upside and this, combined with weaker demand, allowed the copper market to move into a surplus during Q3 2012. ###### Key risks to the price outlook As 2012 draws to a close, we see only minor risks to our full-year average forecast of US$7,913/t (US359¢/lb). Moving into 2013 and beyond, we indicate the upside and downside risks generated by our price model by showing the price forecasts at the 15th and 85th percentile of iterations. With the exception of 2014, the balance of risk is to the upside, reflecting the persistently erratic mine performance in the copper industry, and periodic unexpected outages in the smelting/refining sector. (Historical disruption figures are among the inputs to our model.) We also note that with the market moving into a situation of high surpluses, we expect to see cutbacks at operations and delays to projects, but our estimates may be too conservative. On the downside, macroeconomic and financial risks and their consequent negative impact on consumption could offset the upside risks of lower copper production and higher investor inflows into copper. ###### Production risks Production risks to the price forecast are biased towards the upside. The frequency and variety of outages at mining operations compared to other sectors of the industry are well known, and despite a better year for mine performance in 2012, we have still seen problems with technical failures, labour action and ore grades declining below expectations in certain mines. These risks remain present looking ahead, while incidences of disruption to mines and projects related to “resource nationalism” are on the rise. Alongside the threat from disruption, which we define as an unplanned and u

nexpected outage, the possibility of cutbacks and project delays due to the economic environment has gained strength lately.  Copper miners have enjoyed lengthy periods of the price hovering well above the cost curve in the last decade, and this industry has often been somewhat out of step with the more marginal situation seen by the miners and producers of other metals.  However, cost escalation in the last year has been steep, and miners expressed their concerns to us during LME Week.  With copper prices around the $8,000/t mark, the vast majority of miners will remain profitable, but we are aware that certain mines have operating costs above $6,000/t and as the supply surplus begins
