**recession and activity in key markets in Emerging Europe weakening too, global demand for German exports will suffer.** Also with unemployment now rising for five consecutive months and consumer confidence dropping to a 26-month low, we remain unconvinced that domestic spending will take the slack. **We now forecast growth of just 0.6% this year and next, with a pick-up in 2014 onwards of above 2% growth.** 

Meanwhile, in the UK the Q2 GDP data has been recently revised upwards by 0.2 percentage points to show a 0.5% q/q contraction, with a further upward revision likely at the end of September.  The contraction in Q2 was mostly explained by the extra bank holiday in June, which would point to underlying growth being roughly flat. **Activity data has generally surprised on the upside over the past month** .  Industrial production rebounded strongly in July, while both the manufacturing and services PMIs picked up in August.  This means we now expect a strong rebound in Q

3 GDP data, as the bank holiday effects unwind and the hosting of the Olympics provides a further modest boost. 

Looking ahead, the recent pickup in commodity prices will keep **inflation above target** until early 2013, keeping the consumer sector under pressure, especially when combined with the effects of fiscal austerity. **The export sector will also be held back by a sclerotic Eurozone. Our forecast shows GDP falling by 0.3% this year, before growing just 1.2% in 2013 and around 2.5% a year thereafter.** 

###### **2.2.2 Russia and Eastern Europe: Modest but steady growth** 

Russia had appeared to be performing well in the first half of 2012, with growth driven largely by **consumer spending and underpinned by a strong labour market** .  Retail sales rose by 9.1% y/y over the first seven months of the year, while investment climbed 10.2% during the same period. However, the latest GDP estimate for Q2 indicated that growth had slowed to 4.0% y/y, from 4.9% in the first quarter, somewhat below our expectations.  Although this appears inconsistent with monthly indicators of activity, we have incorporated it into our forecast and **now expect GDP growth of 3.4% this year and slightly lower at 3.3% in 2013.** 

There are signs of **weakness in the more externally exposed manufacturing sector** , and we expect **industrial activity to remain subdued in the near term** .  The main risk to the forecast remains **a sovereign default in parts of the Eurozone,** which would trigger a sharp

Under these circumstances we would expect Chinese policy makers to ease policy swiftly in order to support employment levels. ###### 1. Company mergers and acquisitions 

###### **Cathay Fortune Corp.** 

- **Cathay Fortune Corp.** , a Shanghai based private equity firm announced its offer to acquire all outstanding shares of Australian-listed **Discovery Metals** , that operates the **Boseto** copper mine in Botswana.  The offer values the company at US$847.8m, and represents a 17% premium to the latest settlement price.  If the deal was completed, Cathay Fortune would own 75% of the company, with the remainder held by **China-Africa Development Fund** . The Boseto mine started production in H1 2012, and has a capacity of 34,400t/y of copper. The offer was rejected by Discovery Metals and Cathay Fortune subsequently launched a hostile bid. 

###### **Codelco and Anglo American** 

- On 23<sup>rd</sup> August, **Anglo American** and **Codelco** announced that they had reached a settlement to end a 10-month dispute over Codelco’s use of an option contract in an attempt to acquire Anglo American Sur.  Anglo American will retain control of AA Sur with a reduced, 50.1% shareholding after selling 25.4% of its interest in the company to a new Codelco controlled **Codelco-Mitsui & Co** . joint venture company.  The joint venture will acquire a 29.5% shareholding in AA Sur for US$2.8B after a 4.1% share is transacted away from **Mitsubishi** subject to clearance by Brazilian competition authorities, reducing Mitsubishi’s holding in AA Sur to 20.4%. Mitsubishi will receive US$890M of the total payment plus a fee of US$40M from Anglo American. 

###### **Glencore / Xstrata mega-merger** 

- On 29<sup>th</sup> August, it was reported that a Norwegian sovereign wealth fund, the fourth-largest shareholder in **Xstrata** with 2.97%, would not accept the terms of **Glencore’s** proposed US$30B takeover of Xstrata.  Norway thus joined **Qatar** in demanding improved terms. **Glencore** then upped its offer from 2.80 to 3.05 new shares for each existing Xstrata share. However, under the proposed terms, the current CEO of Glencore, Ivan Glasenberg, would (after 6 months) lead the merged company, rather than Xstrata CEO Mick Davis who had previously been nominated to take charge. The revised deal is valued at US$80B. On 21<sup>st</sup> September, **Xstrata** requested more time from the **UK Takeover Panel** , in order to address shareholder concerns over the proposed merger. They were given until October 1st to agree the final terms of the $80 billion (£49 billion) merger. On 1st October, Xstrata’s board recommended shareholders to accept Glencore’s improved merger terms.  The merger is now awaiting clearance from the EU authorities. 

###### **Zhejiang Hailiang finalises investment in Jinchuan Group** 

- In an agreement signed on 27<sup>th</sup> June, **Zhejiang Hailiang Co. Ltd** ., a manufacturer of copper semi fabricated products, acquired a 1.12% stake in the Chinese copper and nickel producer, **Jinchuan Group*

* . **Hailiang** invested RMB800M (US$127M) into the producer company as it readies for its upcoming IPO in China.  The move toward greater upstream copper processing exposure was attributed to risks associated with **Hailiang’s** high dependence on copper products fabrication and **Jinchuan’s** experience in managing overseas assets.

The extended downtime was purportedly necessitated by problems with the lining of the plant’s flash furnace. The plant is equipped to produce up to 500,000t/y of copper blister from concentrate sourced from the nearby Chuquicamata mine. Last year, the smelter produced an estimated 290,000t of copper blister.

## Appendix D Production forecasting methodology and guide to Chapter 2 & Appendix C tables 

The basis for our forecasts of mine, smelter and refinery production is the CRU Copper Raw Materials Database (CuRMat), which contains operational data for mines, smelters and refineries.  The data are shown in Appendix C, on an operation by operation basis.  These include historical production and planned production at existing operations under ideal operating conditions.  Our detailed table of projects is also included in Appendix C.  The start up year is based on company projections together with CRU’s view on what is technically feasible in the time period allowed. 

###### Operations and projects 

To arrive at our forecasts, firstly we consider planned production from committed operations. This includes all existing operations and projects that are definitely going ahead (ie those that fall into our “firm” category, see below for project definitions) less any planned closures. 

All projects are classified as “firm”, “probable” or “possible” according to the likelihood of them being developed during our five year forecast horizon.  In the short term, this depends on the stage of development of the projects.  The definitions of “firm”, “probable” and “possible” are: 

**Firm** Projects where permitting has been successfully completed and financing is well underway.  Construction may already have started.  Except for unforeseen disasters, these projects should be operating in the very near future, within a maximum of 2-4 years.  It should also be noted that, although these projects are in the final stages, they might very well be held up by other unforeseen factors such as political instability or sharp falls

in the metals prices. 

**Probable** Projects for which the full or bankable feasibility study has started or is well underway and a successful outcome is expected.

Copper Market Outlook October 2012   Appendix D 

**Possible** Feasibility studies have started or are about to start, and there are indications that the economics of the project appear sound.  However, it is not a foregone conclusion at this point that the project will or will not advance to further stages. 

Projects are then classified further according to the type of development, ie greenfield project, brownfield expansion or extension, restart or redevelopment.  There are also a few projects classified as brownfield projects.  This involves the development of a new resource, for example a sulphide orebody at an SXEW operation or the exploitation of a tailings dump at a site where there is already some equipment or infrastructure. 

Firm brownfield expansions and extensions are incorporated into the production figures for the operation and therefore included in the mine-by-mine and country-by-country figures, along with the existing operations.  Restarts at mines which have been closed for less than five years are also included in these figures.  These projects are given a 100% probability of going ahead. However, they are subject to the same standard disruption allowance (see below) as all existing operations. 

Greenfield projects and redevelopments are not included in these figures, due to the higher risks of delays or technical problems.  These projects have been given a 90% probability of going ahead.  These numbers appear in our tables as “committed projects” and the global total is added to the global total (before disruption) for existing operations.  These figures are then subject to the standard disruption allowance. 

A probability factor is applied to the total production that would be expected from probable and possible projects if they are brought on stream.  Probable projects are given a 70% probability of going ahead and the possible projects a 40% probability.  These figures are then subject to the standard disruption allowance. 

###### Disruption allowance 

A disruption allowance is applied to mine production to allow for unforeseen problems, such as strikes, ore grades, adverse weather conditions, earthquakes, technological problems etc.  This disruption allowance is not specific to a particular set of operations; rather it is applied to the industry as a whole based on CRU’s experience. The disruption allowance is independent from any market condition and simply reflects the general production performance of the industry. 

###### Market adjustment 

A bottom line market adjustment is applied whenever we consider that this is justified by market conditions.  Such an adjustment was applied in previous Copper Quarterly Reports because we considered that mine cuts would be necessary to balance the refined copper m

arket, and indeed would occur in response to low prices.  After our Copper Quarterly October 2009 production forecast, our consumption forecasts were revised upwards and we no longer forecasted that prices would fall below the mine cost curve, allowing us to remove the market adjustment for mines.  However, in late 2012, shifts in our estimates for both production and consumption in the medium term outlook resulted in expectations of a significant surplus from 2015.  This surplus is expected to depress prices to the extent that a supply response will be forced, and so from October 2012, we have reinstated the market adjustment, in the forecasts for 2016 and 2017.

The same methodology is applied to smelter and refined output.  In addition, we apply a market adjustment to smelter and refined production to take account of raw material shortages.  This is made after we have considered a reaction to the markets for refined copper and sulphuric acid. As concentrate stocks are now estimated to be critically low, smelter output is lowered to balance the concentrates market.  Refined production then needs to be reduced to balance the blister market.
